<reason>A wins narrowly. A's decision rule — publicly fund prevention, compensation, and labor, but deny objection an unconditional veto — stayed stable across all five speeches and tracked the motion as written. A answered both pressure questions with concrete brakes (pause if killings make establishment unviable; cancel where livelihoods cannot be protected or gains don't exceed alternatives) and a principled account of participation without veto. B was the more rhetorically gifted debater and landed the sharpest mid-debate moves, but B's terminal "redundant or fatal" trap depended on redefining consent as functional cooperation ("consent wearing a frown"), which collides with B's own earlier insistence that communities must be able to answer "not here" — either B requires genuine agreement and loses the objecting-but-workable middle case A identified, or B requires only cooperation and has adopted A's feasibility standard. B's claim that consent is the sole detector of cooperation was asserted, not shown, and B let its injustice and ecological threads fade to bet everything on that one trap.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4's convergence move — converting A's own brakes into "my thesis in their vocabulary" and framing the override as either redundant or fatal — was the most damaging single rebuttal. A5's response was decisive: the approval-vs.-sufficient-cooperation distinction showed the override does real work where a community objects yet implementation remains workable, and B5's "consent wearing a frown" reply conceded the category while relabeling it, leaving B's position caught between abandoning its consent principle or losing the middle case.</best_rebuttal>
